Second Kings opens with a king of Israel lying injured in his palace in ⟦l:samaria_1022|Samaria⟧, after falling through the lattice of an upper room. He sends messengers to ask a foreign god whether he will recover, and on the road they meet a hairy man with a leather belt around his waist. It is the last story of ⟦p:elijah_1131|Elijah⟧, and almost at once his mantle passes to his successor, ⟦p:elisha_1153|Elisha⟧. By the end of the book, some three centuries later, both kingdoms will be gone, ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧ and its temple will lie in ruins, and a descendant of ⟦p:david_994|David⟧ will be eating at the table of the king of ⟦l:babylon_151|Babylon⟧.

First and Second Kings were originally a single work, so this book carries straight on from the last. ⟦p:ahab_113|Ahab⟧ has died in battle at ⟦l:ramoth-gilead_984|Ramoth-gilead⟧, and his son ⟦p:ahaziah_121|Ahaziah⟧ is on the throne of Israel. In Judah, ⟦p:jehoshaphat_808|Jehoshaphat⟧'s long and largely faithful reign is drawing to an end. The two royal houses are allied by marriage, a bond that will bring the worship of ⟦p:baal_573|Baal⟧ into ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧ itself. As before, the writer moves between the two kingdoms, dating each reign by the other, and judging each king by his faithfulness to the Lord. The listener should be warned that the names become confusing. For a time there is a ⟦p:joram_804|Jehoram⟧, also called ⟦p:joram_804|Joram⟧, on both thrones at once, and an Ahaziah in each kingdom too.

The first part of the book belongs to ⟦p:elisha_1153|Elisha⟧. His ministry runs through the reigns of several kings of Israel, and the stories about him are some of the most vivid in the Old Testament: a widow's oil, a Shunammite woman's son, an Aramean general healed in the ⟦l:jordan_653|Jordan⟧, an army struck blind, a besieged city fed overnight. Behind them lies a long struggle with the Arameans of ⟦l:damascus_322|Damascus⟧, first under ⟦p:ben-hadad_453|Ben-hadad⟧ and then under ⟦p:hazael_1463|Hazael⟧, who repeatedly invade Israel. At the centre of these chapters is a violent revolution. ⟦p:jehu_817|Jehu⟧, a commander of Israel's army, is anointed at Elisha's command, and he wipes out the house of ⟦p:ahab_113|Ahab⟧ and the worship of ⟦p:baal_573|Baal⟧ in the north. In Judah, Ahab's daughter ⟦p:athaliah_359|Athaliah⟧ seizes the throne and tries to destroy the line of ⟦p:david_994|David⟧, until a hidden infant prince is brought out of the temple and crowned.

The middle chapters move faster, through a long line of kings. In the eighth century before Christ the northern kingdom enjoys a final season of prosperity under ⟦p:jeroboam_872|Jeroboam⟧ the second, and it was in his days that the prophets Amos and ⟦p:hosea_1555|Hosea⟧ spoke in the north. Then a far greater power arrives. ⟦l:assyria_111|Assyria⟧, from its heartland on the ⟦l:tigris_1163|Tigris⟧ in what is now northern Iraq, begins to march west under a series of formidable kings. Israel's last decades are a chaos of assassinations and shifting alliances, and in chapter seventeen ⟦l:samaria_1022|Samaria⟧ falls. The people of the northern kingdom are deported and scattered, and foreign settlers are brought in to take their place. The writer pauses there for his longest reflection on why it happened.

Judah survives for more than a century longer. Its story now centres on a handful of kings. ⟦p:hezekiah_1512|Hezekiah⟧, a reformer, trusts the Lord when the Assyrian king ⟦p:sennacherib_2489|Sennacherib⟧ surrounds ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧, and the prophet ⟦p:isaiah_617|Isaiah⟧ stands beside him. His son ⟦p:manasseh_1930|Manasseh⟧ reigns longer than any other king of Judah and undoes everything his father did. ⟦p:josiah_1730|Josiah⟧, who came to the throne as a boy of eight, repairs the temple, where the book of the law is found, and leads the most thorough reform in Judah's history. The prophet ⟦p:jeremiah_853|Jeremiah⟧ began his work in Josiah's reign, and much of his book belongs in the final chapters here.

By then ⟦l:assyria_111|Assyria⟧ itself has fallen, and ⟦l:babylon_151|Babylon⟧ has taken its place. ⟦p:josiah_1730|Josiah⟧ dies in battle, and his sons and grandson are caught between ⟦l:egypt_362|Egypt⟧ and Babylon. ⟦p:nebuchadnezzar_2167|Nebuchadnezzar⟧, king of Babylon, takes ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧ in two stages. First the young king ⟦p:jehoiachin_791|Jehoiachin⟧ is carried off with the leading citizens, among them the priest ⟦p:ezekiel_1237|Ezekiel⟧. Eleven years later, after the last king, ⟦p:zedekiah_1950|Zedekiah⟧, rebels, the city is besieged, the temple is burned and the walls are broken down.

The book does not end in silence, though. Its final paragraph moves forward to the thirty-seventh year of exile, when a new king of ⟦l:babylon_151|Babylon⟧ releases ⟦p:jehoiachin_791|Jehoiachin⟧ from prison and gives him a place at his table. The line of ⟦p:david_994|David⟧ has not been extinguished. The books of Chronicles retell much of this history from another angle, and the story of the return from exile is taken up in ⟦p:ezra_1245|Ezra⟧ and Nehemiah. Many of the prophetic books, from Amos to ⟦p:jeremiah_853|Jeremiah⟧, belong inside the years this book describes.

⟦p:ahab_113|Ahab⟧ is dead, killed by an arrow at ⟦l:ramoth-gilead_984|Ramoth-gilead⟧, and his son ⟦p:ahaziah_120|Ahaziah⟧ now rules Israel from ⟦l:samaria_1022|Samaria⟧. The chapter opens with a brief note that ⟦l:moab_815|Moab⟧, the kingdom east of the Dead Sea, has seized the moment to throw off Israel's rule. That rebellion will be taken up again in chapter three.

⟦p:ahaziah_120|Ahaziah⟧ has fallen through the lattice of an upper room and is badly hurt. He sends messengers to consult ⟦p:baal-zebub_579|Baal-zebub⟧, the god of the Philistine city of ⟦l:ekron_364|Ekron⟧, near the coast, to ask whether he will recover. The name means lord of the flies. For a king of Israel, the choice says everything.

The messengers never reach ⟦l:ekron_364|Ekron⟧. They are met on the road by a man whose description the king recognises at once, and the rest of the chapter is a confrontation between the king and the prophet in which the king sends soldiers three times. It is the last time we see ⟦p:elijah_1131|Elijah⟧ confronting the house of ⟦p:ahab_113|Ahab⟧. The chapter ends with a succession, and with the first of the book's confusing names: ⟦p:ahaziah_120|Ahaziah⟧'s brother ⟦p:joram_804|Jehoram⟧ takes the throne of Israel, while another Jehoram, the son of ⟦p:jehoshaphat_808|Jehoshaphat⟧, is reigning in Judah.
2:
This chapter belongs to the hand-over between two prophets. It opens by telling the listener what is about to happen: the Lord is going to take ⟦p:elijah_1131|Elijah⟧ up to heaven in a whirlwind. ⟦p:elisha_1153|Elisha⟧, the farmer Elijah called from the plough, has been his servant ever since, and the prophets along the way all know that today is the day.

⟦p:elijah_1131|Elijah⟧ sets out on a last journey, from ⟦l:gilgal_476|Gilgal⟧ to ⟦l:bethel_202|Bethel⟧, then down to ⟦l:jericho_634|Jericho⟧, and finally to the ⟦l:jordan_653|Jordan⟧. At each stop he tells ⟦p:elisha_1153|Elisha⟧ to stay behind, and at each stop Elisha refuses. Along the way we meet the sons of the prophets, communities of prophets living together at Bethel and Jericho, who will appear often in the Elisha stories. At the river, Elijah's cloak plays the part that ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧' staff once played at the ⟦l:red_sea_986|Red Sea⟧, and the two men cross on dry ground, into the country where Moses himself was taken from Israel. Elisha's request on the far bank is for a double portion of his master's spirit, the inheritance of a firstborn son.

What happens next made ⟦p:elijah_1131|Elijah⟧ a figure of expectation for centuries; the prophet ⟦p:malachi_1899|Malachi⟧ spoke of his return, and the Gospels take up that hope. The rest of the chapter shows ⟦p:elisha_1153|Elisha⟧ beginning his own work, at ⟦l:jericho_634|Jericho⟧ and at ⟦l:bethel_202|Bethel⟧, with the same authority, and the same severity, as his master.
3:
⟦p:elisha_1153|Elisha⟧ has begun his ministry, and the writer now turns to the reign of ⟦p:joram_804|Jehoram⟧ son of ⟦p:ahab_113|Ahab⟧, king of Israel, also called ⟦p:joram_804|Joram⟧. He is not as bad as his parents, Ahab and ⟦p:jezebel_1605|Jezebel⟧, and he removes the pillar of ⟦p:baal_573|Baal⟧ his father set up, but he keeps ⟦p:jeroboam_872|Jeroboam⟧'s calves.

The chapter takes up the rebellion of ⟦l:moab_815|Moab⟧ mentioned at the start of chapter one. Moab lay on the high plateau east of the Dead Sea, and its king, ⟦p:mesha_2009|Mesha⟧, had been paying Israel a heavy tribute in lambs and wool. Remarkably, Mesha's own account of his revolt has survived. A black basalt stone found in the nineteenth century, now known as the Moabite Stone, records his victory over Israel and even names Omri.

⟦p:joram_804|Jehoram⟧ sets out to bring ⟦l:moab_815|Moab⟧ back under control. He calls on ⟦p:jehoshaphat_808|Jehoshaphat⟧ of Judah, who answers in the same words he once used to ⟦p:ahab_113|Ahab⟧, and the king of ⟦l:edom_357|Edom⟧, a land then under Judah's control. The three armies march by a long route around the southern end of the Dead Sea, and in the desert their water runs out. Jehoshaphat asks, as he did before ⟦l:ramoth-gilead_984|Ramoth-gilead⟧, whether there is a prophet of the Lord nearby. There is: ⟦p:elisha_1153|Elisha⟧. The campaign ends on the walls of the Moabite city of Kir-haraseth, with a desperate act by its king.
4:
The battles of chapter three are left behind, and the book now gathers a series of stories about ⟦p:elisha_1153|Elisha⟧'s ministry among ordinary people, while the kings fade into the background. Here the prophet's concern is with widows, children and hungry communities.

The first story concerns the widow of one of the sons of the prophets, whose creditor is about to take her two sons as slaves to pay off a debt, as the law of the time allowed. The second, and the longest, takes us to ⟦l:shunem_1089|Shunem⟧, a village in the ⟦l:jezreel_643|Jezreel⟧ valley in the north. A wealthy woman there has noticed the prophet passing by, and she and her husband build him a small room on their roof. We also meet ⟦p:elisha_1153|Elisha⟧'s servant ⟦p:gehazi_1293|Gehazi⟧, who will appear in several stories to come. The Shunammite woman will return later in the book, so her story is worth following closely.

Two shorter episodes follow among the prophets, the first at ⟦l:gilgal_476|Gilgal⟧ in a time of famine. One involves a pot of stew, and the other twenty loaves of barley bread and a hundred hungry men. Readers of the Gospels will hear an echo of that last story in the feeding of the crowds by ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧.
5:
⟦p:elisha_1153|Elisha⟧'s fame has spread, even beyond Israel's borders. This chapter takes us first to ⟦l:damascus_322|Damascus⟧, the capital of ⟦l:syria_1122|Aram⟧, Israel's great rival to the north-east. Its army is commanded by ⟦p:naaman_2122|Naaman⟧, a celebrated soldier and a favourite of the king, and the writer makes a striking remark: it was through him that the Lord had given Aram victory. But Naaman has a skin disease, the kind the Bible calls leprosy, which could make a man an outcast.

The story turns on someone with no name and no power at all, an Israelite girl captured in a border raid who now serves ⟦p:naaman_2122|Naaman⟧'s wife. She knows of a prophet in ⟦l:samaria_1022|Samaria⟧. What follows involves two kings, a diplomatic letter that causes alarm in Israel, and a great man arriving with horses and chariots at the door of ⟦p:elisha_1153|Elisha⟧'s house, expecting to be received with ceremony.

⟦p:naaman_2122|Naaman⟧'s journey ends at the river ⟦l:jordan_653|Jordan⟧, but the chapter does not end there. ⟦p:elisha_1153|Elisha⟧'s servant ⟦p:gehazi_1293|Gehazi⟧, whom we met at ⟦l:shunem_1089|Shunem⟧, has his own ideas about Naaman's gifts. Centuries later, in the synagogue at ⟦l:nazareth_878|Nazareth⟧, ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ would remind his hearers that there were many lepers in Israel in Elisha's day, yet the one who was cleansed was Naaman the Syrian.

After the story of Naaman, the writer returns briefly to the community of prophets gathered around ⟦p:elisha_1153|Elisha⟧. They have outgrown their meeting place and go down to the ⟦l:jordan_653|Jordan⟧ to cut timber for a new one. A small accident with a borrowed axe head shows the prophet's care for a poor man's loss.

Then the scene widens again to the war between Israel and ⟦l:syria_1122|Aram⟧, which in these years took the form of constant raids across the border. The king of Israel is not named in these stories. The king of Aram finds that his plans are known in ⟦l:samaria_1022|Samaria⟧ before he can carry them out, and he discovers why. He sends a force to capture ⟦p:elisha_1153|Elisha⟧ at ⟦l:dothan_342|Dothan⟧, a town on the road north of Samaria, the place where, long ago, ⟦p:joseph_1710|Joseph⟧'s brothers sold him. Elisha's frightened servant is about to see something hidden from ordinary eyes.

The last part of the chapter, which runs straight on into the next, takes place in very different circumstances. ⟦p:ben-hadad_453|Ben-hadad⟧, king of ⟦l:syria_1122|Aram⟧, brings his whole army to besiege ⟦l:samaria_1022|Samaria⟧, and the famine inside the walls becomes desperate. The king of Israel, walking the wall in sackcloth, hears something that drives him to blame ⟦p:elisha_1153|Elisha⟧, and he sends a man to take his life.
7:
⟦l:samaria_1022|Samaria⟧ is starving under the Aramean siege, and the king has just sent a messenger to ⟦p:elisha_1153|Elisha⟧'s house, blaming the Lord, and the prophet, for the disaster. This chapter follows straight on from the last, and it opens with Elisha's answer.

He announces that by this time tomorrow, food will be sold cheaply at the gate of ⟦l:samaria_1022|Samaria⟧. The royal officer on whose arm the king leans mocks the very idea, and ⟦p:elisha_1153|Elisha⟧ gives him a personal word of his own.

Then the story moves outside the city walls, to four men with leprosy sitting at the gate. Barred from the city by their disease and starving like everyone else, they decide they have nothing left to lose by walking over to the enemy camp. They set out at twilight. What they find, and what they decide to do about it, brings the siege to an end in a way no one in ⟦l:samaria_1022|Samaria⟧ could have planned. The chapter closes by returning to the officer at the gate, and the writer takes care to show that every part of ⟦p:elisha_1153|Elisha⟧'s word came true.
8:
The chapter opens with a story that reaches back to an earlier time. The woman of ⟦l:shunem_1089|Shunem⟧, whose son ⟦p:elisha_1153|Elisha⟧ raised to life, was warned by the prophet of a coming seven-year famine and left the country to live among the Philistines. Now she has returned to find her house and land taken over, and she comes to the king to appeal. She arrives just as ⟦p:gehazi_1293|Gehazi⟧ is telling the king about Elisha's deeds.

Then the scene shifts to ⟦l:damascus_322|Damascus⟧. Years before, at Mount Horeb, the Lord told ⟦p:elijah_1131|Elijah⟧ to anoint ⟦p:hazael_1463|Hazael⟧ as king of ⟦l:syria_1122|Aram⟧. Now ⟦p:elisha_1153|Elisha⟧ goes to Damascus, where ⟦p:ben-hadad_453|Ben-hadad⟧ the king lies ill, and Hazael comes to meet him with a question from his master. Elisha's answer, and what he sees in Hazael's face, are among the most haunting moments in his story. Assyrian records call Hazael the son of a nobody.

The last part of the chapter returns to Judah. ⟦p:jehoram_803|Jehoram⟧ son of ⟦p:jehoshaphat_808|Jehoshaphat⟧ now reigns in ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧, and he has married a daughter of ⟦p:ahab_113|Ahab⟧. Her name is ⟦p:athaliah_359|Athaliah⟧. Their son ⟦p:ahaziah_121|Ahaziah⟧ succeeds him, and joins his uncle, ⟦p:joram_804|Joram⟧ of Israel, in another war against ⟦l:syria_1122|Aram⟧ at ⟦l:ramoth-gilead_984|Ramoth-gilead⟧, the same town where Ahab died. 9:
Two kings are at ⟦l:jezreel_643|Jezreel⟧: ⟦p:joram_804|Joram⟧ son of ⟦p:ahab_113|Ahab⟧, king of Israel, recovering from wounds taken in battle with the Arameans, and his nephew ⟦p:ahaziah_121|Ahaziah⟧, king of Judah, who has come to visit him. Israel's army remains in the field at ⟦l:ramoth-gilead_984|Ramoth-gilead⟧, east of the ⟦l:jordan_653|Jordan⟧, under its commanders. One of them is ⟦p:jehu_817|Jehu⟧ son of ⟦p:nimshi_2207|Nimshi⟧.

Years earlier, at Horeb, ⟦p:elijah_1131|Elijah⟧ was told to anoint ⟦p:jehu_817|Jehu⟧ as king of Israel. Elijah never did it himself. Now ⟦p:elisha_1153|Elisha⟧ sends a young man from the company of prophets with a flask of oil and very precise instructions, including the instruction to run as soon as he has finished. Jehu's fellow officers respond at once.

What follows is told at a gallop, and the narrator lets ⟦p:jehu_817|Jehu⟧'s furious chariot driving set the pace. From the watchtower at ⟦l:jezreel_643|Jezreel⟧ the approaching troops are seen in the distance, and messengers ride out to ask the same question again and again: is it peace? The confrontation that ends the reign takes place, of all places, on the plot of ground that once belonged to ⟦p:naboth_2127|Naboth⟧, the man ⟦p:ahab_113|Ahab⟧ and ⟦p:jezebel_1605|Jezebel⟧ had killed for his vineyard, and the words ⟦p:elijah_1131|Elijah⟧ spoke against them there are remembered. 10:
⟦p:joram_804|Joram⟧, ⟦p:ahaziah_121|Ahaziah⟧ and ⟦p:jezebel_1605|Jezebel⟧ are dead, and ⟦p:jehu_817|Jehu⟧ holds ⟦l:jezreel_643|Jezreel⟧. But the house of ⟦p:ahab_113|Ahab⟧ is large. Seventy of Ahab's descendants are being brought up in ⟦l:samaria_1022|Samaria⟧, the capital, under the care of its leading men, and any of them could become a rallying point against the new king.

⟦p:jehu_817|Jehu⟧ moves against them by letter, and then against everyone connected with ⟦p:ahab_113|Ahab⟧'s rule, and even against a party of ⟦p:ahaziah_121|Ahaziah⟧'s relatives from Judah whom he meets on the road. Along the way he picks up an ally, ⟦p:jonadab_799|Jehonadab⟧ son of ⟦p:rechab_2403|Rechab⟧, the founder of a strict and austere clan who will reappear generations later in the book of ⟦p:jeremiah_853|Jeremiah⟧. Then Jehu turns to the worship of ⟦p:baal_573|Baal⟧ itself, which Ahab and ⟦p:jezebel_1605|Jezebel⟧ brought into Israel, with a plan that depends on deception.

The writer's final verdict on ⟦p:jehu_817|Jehu⟧ is mixed. He destroys ⟦p:baal_573|Baal⟧ worship in Israel, and the Lord promises his descendants the throne for four generations, but he keeps the golden calves of ⟦p:jeroboam_872|Jeroboam⟧. A century later the prophet ⟦p:hosea_1555|Hosea⟧ would speak of the blood shed at ⟦l:jezreel_643|Jezreel⟧ as a debt still owed. Assyrian records add a detail the Bible does not give: a black stone monument of the Assyrian king Shalmaneser records the tribute of Jehu and shows an Israelite bowing to the ground before him. Meanwhile, in the east, ⟦p:hazael_1463|Hazael⟧ of ⟦l:damascus_322|Damascus⟧ begins to take Israel's lands beyond the ⟦l:jordan_653|Jordan⟧.
11:
⟦p:jehu_817|Jehu⟧'s revolution has left the throne of Judah empty, for ⟦p:ahaziah_121|Ahaziah⟧ king of Judah was killed in the same purge. His mother, ⟦p:athaliah_359|Athaliah⟧, the daughter of ⟦p:ahab_113|Ahab⟧, is now in ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧, and she sees her chance. She sets out to destroy the entire royal family, her own grandchildren among them, and takes the throne for herself. For six years Judah is ruled by a queen from the house of Ahab, the only time in its history that a ruler not descended from ⟦p:david_994|David⟧ sat on the throne.

But one child escapes. ⟦p:ahaziah_121|Ahaziah⟧'s sister ⟦p:jehoshabeath_811|Jehosheba⟧ rescues his infant son ⟦p:joash_1632|Joash⟧ and hides him, with his nurse, in the house of the Lord. The book of Chronicles tells us that she was the wife of ⟦p:jehoiada_793|Jehoiada⟧, the chief priest, which explains how the boy could be kept hidden within the temple precincts for so long.

In the seventh year, ⟦p:jehoiada_793|Jehoiada⟧ acts. He takes the captains of the royal guard into his confidence and lays his plans carefully around the changing of the guard on the Sabbath. The chapter tells of the day the hidden prince is brought out, with ⟦p:david_994|David⟧'s own spears and shields in the hands of the guard. The promise of a lamp for David in ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧ has come down, for a time, to a single child of seven.
12:
⟦p:joash_1632|Joash⟧, the boy who was hidden in the temple, has been crowned at the age of seven and is now king of Judah. He will reign for forty years. The writer's verdict on him comes with a careful qualification: he did what was right in the eyes of the Lord all the days that ⟦p:jehoiada_793|Jehoiada⟧ the priest instructed him.

The main business of his reign, as Kings tells it, is the repair of the temple, which had fallen into disrepair and, Chronicles tells us, had been plundered by ⟦p:athaliah_359|Athaliah⟧'s sons for the worship of ⟦p:baal_573|Baal⟧. ⟦p:joash_1632|Joash⟧ orders the priests to use the temple's income for the work, but years pass and nothing is done. The solution, in the twenty-third year of his reign, is a simple collection chest with a hole bored in the lid, set beside the altar.

The end of the reign is darker. ⟦p:hazael_1463|Hazael⟧ of ⟦l:damascus_322|Damascus⟧, who has already taken Israel's lands east of the ⟦l:jordan_653|Jordan⟧, captures the Philistine city of ⟦l:gath_442|Gath⟧ and then turns toward ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧, and ⟦p:joash_1632|Joash⟧ buys him off with the temple's treasures. Chronicles also records more of these later years, including the stoning of ⟦p:jehoiada_793|Jehoiada⟧'s son Zechariah after the old priest's death. Kings notes only that Joash's own servants conspired against him and killed him.
13:
The story crosses back to the northern kingdom, where ⟦p:jehu_817|Jehu⟧'s son ⟦p:jehoahaz_784|Jehoahaz⟧ now reigns in ⟦l:samaria_1022|Samaria⟧. These are dark years for Israel. ⟦p:hazael_1463|Hazael⟧ of ⟦l:damascus_322|Damascus⟧, whose future cruelty ⟦p:elisha_1153|Elisha⟧ foresaw with tears, presses Israel so hard that its army is reduced to a remnant, like dust at threshing time. When Jehoahaz seeks the Lord, a deliverer is sent, though the writer does not say who it was.

⟦p:jehoahaz_784|Jehoahaz⟧ is followed by his son ⟦p:joash_1633|Jehoash⟧. The names are tangled again here: Jehoash of Israel reigns at the same time as ⟦p:joash_1633|Joash⟧ of Judah, the boy king of chapter eleven, now a grown man. The writer summarises Jehoash's reign almost at once, and then steps back to tell one more story from it.

⟦p:elisha_1153|Elisha⟧ is dying. He has been a prophet for more than half a century, since the days of ⟦p:ahab_113|Ahab⟧, through the reigns of ⟦p:joram_804|Joram⟧, ⟦p:jehu_817|Jehu⟧, ⟦p:jehoahaz_784|Jehoahaz⟧ and now ⟦p:joash_1633|Jehoash⟧, though he has not appeared in the story since Jehu's anointing. The young king comes to his bedside and weeps, crying out the same words Elisha himself once cried as ⟦p:elijah_1131|Elijah⟧ was taken up: my father, my father, the chariots and horsemen of Israel. The prophet's last act involves a bow, some arrows and an open window facing east, toward ⟦l:syria_1122|Aram⟧. Even after his burial, the writer has one more remarkable story to tell about Elisha's tomb.
14:
The book returns to Judah, where ⟦p:amaziah_214|Amaziah⟧, the son of ⟦p:joash_1633|Joash⟧, takes the throne. He is judged to have done right, though not like ⟦p:david_994|David⟧. He punishes his father's murderers, sparing their children as the law of ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧ required, and he wins a victory over ⟦l:edom_357|Edom⟧ in the south.

Flushed with success, he challenges ⟦p:joash_1633|Jehoash⟧, king of Israel, who replies with a mocking fable about a thistle and a cedar. ⟦p:amaziah_214|Amaziah⟧ will not listen, and the battle at ⟦l:beth-shemesh_234|Beth-shemesh⟧, in the low hills west of ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧, ends in a humiliation for Judah that reaches the walls and the treasures of Jerusalem itself. Amaziah later dies, like his father, at the hands of conspirators.

The chapter closes in the north with the long reign of ⟦p:jeroboam_873|Jeroboam⟧ son of ⟦p:joash_1633|Jehoash⟧, often called Jeroboam the second. For forty-one years he reigns in ⟦l:samaria_1022|Samaria⟧, and with ⟦l:damascus_322|Damascus⟧ weakened and ⟦l:assyria_111|Assyria⟧ not yet pressing west, he restores Israel's borders almost to their extent in ⟦p:solomon_2762|Solomon⟧'s day. The writer notes that this was foretold by a prophet named ⟦p:jonah_1689|Jonah⟧ son of ⟦p:amittai_219|Amittai⟧, from ⟦l:gath-hepher_443|Gath-hepher⟧ in ⟦l:galilee_433|Galilee⟧, the same Jonah whose book tells of his mission to ⟦l:nineveh_899|Nineveh⟧. Jeroboam's reign was a time of wealth for some and injustice for many, and it was in these years that Amos and ⟦p:hosea_1555|Hosea⟧ delivered their warnings to the north.
15:
This chapter covers half a century and a long line of kings at a rapid pace. In Judah, there is stability. ⟦p:uzziah_375|Azariah⟧, also called ⟦p:uzziah_375|Uzziah⟧, reigns for fifty-two years, and his son ⟦p:jotham_1735|Jotham⟧ after him. Azariah is struck with a skin disease, and for his last years Jotham governs on his behalf. It was in the year King Uzziah died, the book of ⟦p:isaiah_617|Isaiah⟧ tells us, that Isaiah saw the Lord in the temple and received his call.

In Israel, it is the opposite. After the death of ⟦p:jeroboam_872|Jeroboam⟧ the second, the northern kingdom slides into chaos. His son ⟦p:zachariah_2969|Zechariah⟧ reigns six months before he is assassinated, and with him ⟦p:jehu_817|Jehu⟧'s dynasty ends, after the four generations promised. ⟦p:shallum_2514|Shallum⟧ lasts one month. ⟦p:menahem_1996|Menahem⟧ seizes power with great brutality, ⟦p:pekahiah_2300|Pekahiah⟧ his son is murdered by one of his own officers, ⟦p:pekah_2299|Pekah⟧, and Pekah himself is killed by ⟦p:hoshea_1559|Hoshea⟧. Four of Israel's last six kings die by assassination. The prophet ⟦p:hosea_1555|Hosea⟧, speaking in these years, complains that Israel sets up kings without the Lord's consent.

Over all this falls the shadow of ⟦l:assyria_111|Assyria⟧. Its king ⟦p:tilgath-pilneser_2376|Tiglath-pileser⟧, here first called ⟦p:tilgath-pilneser_2376|Pul⟧, appears in the land, and ⟦p:menahem_1996|Menahem⟧ pays him a vast sum to keep his throne. Under ⟦p:pekah_2299|Pekah⟧, Tiglath-pileser returns, takes ⟦l:galilee_433|Galilee⟧ and ⟦l:gilead_475|Gilead⟧, and deports their people. The chapter closes with a warning: ⟦p:rezin_2435|Rezin⟧ of ⟦l:damascus_322|Damascus⟧ and Pekah of Israel have begun to move against Judah.
16:
⟦p:jotham_1735|Jotham⟧ has died, and his son ⟦p:ahaz_118|Ahaz⟧ reigns in ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧. He is the first king of Judah since ⟦p:ahaziah_121|Ahaziah⟧, the grandson of ⟦p:ahab_113|Ahab⟧, to be judged as doing wrong, and the writer records that he even offers his own son in the fire, a practice of the surrounding nations.

The threat at the end of chapter fifteen now arrives. ⟦p:rezin_2435|Rezin⟧, king of ⟦l:syria_1122|Aram⟧, and ⟦p:pekah_2299|Pekah⟧, king of Israel, march on ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧ and besiege it, meaning, as ⟦p:isaiah_617|Isaiah⟧ tells us, to put a king of their own choosing on its throne. The book of Isaiah, in its seventh chapter, describes the same crisis from inside the city: the king's heart shaking like trees in the wind, and the prophet sent to meet him with a sign and a call to trust the Lord.

⟦p:ahaz_118|Ahaz⟧ chooses another course. He sends silver and gold to ⟦p:tilgath-pilneser_2376|Tiglath-pileser⟧, king of ⟦l:assyria_111|Assyria⟧, with a message calling himself the Assyrian king's servant and son. Assyria answers by capturing ⟦l:damascus_322|Damascus⟧ and ending its kingdom. When Ahaz goes to Damascus to meet his new overlord, he sees an altar there, and the rest of the chapter describes the changes he makes to the temple in ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧ on his return. Among the things he takes apart are the bronze stands and the great Sea that ⟦p:solomon_2762|Solomon⟧'s craftsman made.
17:
⟦l:damascus_322|Damascus⟧ has fallen to ⟦l:assyria_111|Assyria⟧, and ⟦l:galilee_433|Galilee⟧ and ⟦l:gilead_475|Gilead⟧ have been stripped from Israel. What remains of the northern kingdom is little more than the hill country around ⟦l:samaria_1022|Samaria⟧, ruled by ⟦p:hoshea_1559|Hoshea⟧, the man who murdered ⟦p:pekah_2299|Pekah⟧. He will be Israel's last king.

⟦l:assyria_111|Assyria⟧ is now ruled by Shalmaneser, the son of ⟦p:tilgath-pilneser_2376|Tiglath-pileser⟧, and ⟦p:hoshea_1559|Hoshea⟧ becomes his vassal, paying tribute. Then he gambles on rebellion, sending envoys to So, king of ⟦l:egypt_362|Egypt⟧, and withholding the tribute. Assyria's response is swift. The siege of ⟦l:samaria_1022|Samaria⟧ lasts three years, and when the city falls, around seven hundred and twenty-two years before Christ, its people are carried away to distant parts of the Assyrian empire, in northern ⟦l:mesopotamia_790|Mesopotamia⟧ and the mountains of the ⟦l:media_776|Medes⟧. Assyrian records credit the final conquest to Shalmaneser's successor, Sargon.

The writer then does something he has done nowhere else in Kings. He stops the narrative to explain, at length, why this happened, gathering up the warnings of the prophets and the long history of the sins of ⟦p:jeroboam_872|Jeroboam⟧. The final part of the chapter describes the peoples ⟦l:assyria_111|Assyria⟧ brought in from elsewhere to resettle the land, and the mixed worship that grew up among them. Their descendants, the Samaritans, will still be living in these hills in the time of the Gospels, and still regarded with suspicion in ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧.
18:
With the northern kingdom gone, the rest of Second Kings belongs to ⟦l:judah-southern_1281|Judah⟧ alone. It begins with one of its finest kings. ⟦p:hezekiah_1512|Hezekiah⟧, the son of ⟦p:ahaz_118|Ahaz⟧, comes to the throne in ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧, and the writer's praise for him is unusually warm: no king of Judah was like him in his trust in the Lord. He removes the high places that earlier good kings left standing, and even breaks up the bronze snake ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧ made in the wilderness, to which the people have been burning incense.

⟦p:hezekiah_1512|Hezekiah⟧ also rebels against ⟦l:assyria_111|Assyria⟧, refusing to pay the tribute his father agreed. The fall of ⟦l:samaria_1022|Samaria⟧, retold briefly here from ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧'s side of the border, shows what that could mean. In the fourteenth year of his reign, about seven hundred and one years before Christ, the Assyrian king ⟦p:sennacherib_2489|Sennacherib⟧ invades ⟦l:judah-southern_1281|Judah⟧ and takes its fortified towns one by one. Sennacherib's own annals boast of shutting Hezekiah up in Jerusalem like a bird in a cage, and carved stone panels from his palace at ⟦l:nineveh_899|Nineveh⟧, now in the British Museum, show the siege of ⟦l:lachish_711|Lachish⟧, Judah's second city.

⟦p:hezekiah_1512|Hezekiah⟧ pays a heavy price to end the invasion, but the Assyrians come anyway. Three high officials arrive outside ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧, and their spokesman, the ⟦p:rabshakeh_2384|Rabshakeh⟧, addresses the city in Hebrew, so that the people on the wall will understand. His speech is a masterpiece of intimidation.
19:
The ⟦p:rabshakeh_2384|Rabshakeh⟧'s words have been reported to ⟦p:hezekiah_1512|Hezekiah⟧, and his officials stand before him with their clothes torn. The king's response is to go into the house of the Lord, and to send for the prophet ⟦p:isaiah_617|Isaiah⟧ son of ⟦p:amoz_240|Amoz⟧. Isaiah has been speaking to the kings of Judah since the year of ⟦p:uzziah_375|Uzziah⟧'s death, and the book that bears his name contains these same events, told in almost the same words.

The Assyrian army is still at work elsewhere in Judah, and a new danger appears from the south: an Egyptian army led by ⟦p:tirhakah_2865|Tirhakah⟧, of the Cushite line of pharaohs from the upper ⟦l:nile_895|Nile⟧. ⟦p:sennacherib_2489|Sennacherib⟧ sends ⟦p:hezekiah_1512|Hezekiah⟧ a letter, repeating his challenge. Hezekiah takes the letter into the temple, spreads it out before the Lord, and prays.

⟦p:isaiah_617|Isaiah⟧'s answer, much of it in poetry, is addressed not only to ⟦p:hezekiah_1512|Hezekiah⟧ but to the Assyrian king himself, and it answers his boasts with the Lord's own words. ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧'s deliverance, when it comes, is told in a single sentence, followed by ⟦p:sennacherib_2489|Sennacherib⟧'s return to ⟦l:nineveh_899|Nineveh⟧. Its final lines leap forward some twenty years to the manner of his death.
20:
⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧ has been delivered from the Assyrians. Now the book steps back to tell two more stories from ⟦p:hezekiah_1512|Hezekiah⟧'s reign, from the days when the Assyrian threat still hung over the city.

⟦p:hezekiah_1512|Hezekiah⟧ falls mortally ill, and ⟦p:isaiah_617|Isaiah⟧ brings him a blunt message: put your house in order, for you will not recover. What follows involves a prayer, a poultice of figs, and a sign on the stairway of ⟦p:ahaz_118|Ahaz⟧, Hezekiah's father, where a shadow marked the passing of the day.

The second story brings a new name into the book. Envoys arrive from ⟦p:merodach-baladan_483|Merodach-baladan⟧, king of ⟦l:babylon_151|Babylon⟧, a long-time rebel against Assyrian rule, who has heard of ⟦p:hezekiah_1512|Hezekiah⟧'s illness. Babylon is still a restless subject of ⟦l:assyria_111|Assyria⟧, not yet a great power. Hezekiah welcomes the envoys warmly and shows them everything he has. ⟦p:isaiah_617|Isaiah⟧'s response looks far ahead, more than a century, to the day when Babylon will take it all away. Last comes a mention of the tunnel Hezekiah cut to bring water into the city. It can still be walked today, and an inscription found inside it describes the moment the two teams of diggers met.
21:
⟦p:hezekiah_1512|Hezekiah⟧ has died, and his son ⟦p:manasseh_1930|Manasseh⟧ comes to the throne at the age of twelve. He will reign for fifty-five years, longer than any other king of Judah or Israel, and the writer judges him more harshly than any other.

These were the years when ⟦l:assyria_111|Assyria⟧ was at the height of its power, under ⟦p:sennacherib_2489|Sennacherib⟧'s son Esarhaddon and grandson Ashurbanipal, and Assyrian records list ⟦p:manasseh_1930|Manasseh⟧ among the loyal kings who paid them tribute. Inside Judah, he reverses everything his father did. He rebuilds the high places, raises altars to ⟦p:baal_573|Baal⟧, and sets up altars to the stars in the very courts of the temple, and he is remembered for shedding innocent blood throughout ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧. The writer compares him explicitly to ⟦p:ahab_113|Ahab⟧, the king who brought Baal into ⟦l:samaria_1022|Samaria⟧.

The Lord's response comes through unnamed prophets, and now it is declared plainly that ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧ will go the way of ⟦l:samaria_1022|Samaria⟧. The book of Chronicles adds that ⟦p:manasseh_1930|Manasseh⟧ was later taken captive to ⟦l:babylon_151|Babylon⟧ and humbled himself before the Lord, but Kings does not mention it. After Manasseh comes the short reign of his son ⟦p:amon_236|Amon⟧, who follows his father's ways and is murdered by his own servants. The people of the land put his eight-year-old son on the throne. His name is ⟦p:josiah_1730|Josiah⟧.
22:
⟦p:josiah_1730|Josiah⟧, the boy king, has now reigned for eighteen years and is twenty-six years old. Three centuries earlier, a man of God stood at ⟦p:jeroboam_872|Jeroboam⟧'s altar in ⟦l:bethel_202|Bethel⟧ and spoke his name. He is the last great king of Judah, and the writer praises him without reservation: he did not turn aside to the right or to the left.

⟦l:assyria_111|Assyria⟧'s grip on the west is weakening in these years, giving Judah room to act. It was also in ⟦p:josiah_1730|Josiah⟧'s reign that a young man from a priestly family at Anathoth, ⟦p:jeremiah_853|Jeremiah⟧, received his call to be a prophet, and the prophet Zephaniah was speaking in ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧ too.

The chapter begins with the repair of the temple, arranged much as it was in the days of ⟦p:joash_1632|Joash⟧, through the king's secretary ⟦p:shaphan_2550|Shaphan⟧ and ⟦p:hilkiah_1524|Hilkiah⟧ the high priest. In the course of the work, Hilkiah finds something in the house of the Lord: the Book of the Law. When Shaphan reads it aloud to the king, ⟦p:josiah_1730|Josiah⟧'s response is immediate, and he sends to inquire of the Lord. The answer comes through a woman, the prophetess ⟦p:huldah_1567|Huldah⟧, who lives in the Second District of ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧.
23:
⟦p:huldah_1567|Huldah⟧'s words have been brought to the king: judgement will come on ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧, but not in ⟦p:josiah_1730|Josiah⟧'s lifetime. Josiah calls the elders and all the people to the temple, reads the book aloud to them, and leads them into a covenant to keep its words.

Then comes the most thorough reform in the history of ⟦l:judah-southern_1281|Judah⟧. The chapter reads like an inventory of three centuries of accumulated idolatry, removed, broken and burned. Some of it goes back to ⟦p:manasseh_1930|Manasseh⟧ and ⟦p:ahaz_118|Ahaz⟧, some to ⟦p:solomon_2762|Solomon⟧ himself, whose shrines east of ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧ are still standing. It reaches north to ⟦l:bethel_202|Bethel⟧, where ⟦p:jeroboam_872|Jeroboam⟧'s altar still stands, and there the word spoken by the man of God in First Kings is fulfilled in detail. The reform ends with a Passover kept as it had not been kept since the days of the judges.

Yet the writer adds a sombre note: even this did not turn aside the Lord's anger over ⟦p:manasseh_1930|Manasseh⟧. The last part of the chapter is set in a changing world. ⟦l:nineveh_899|Nineveh⟧, the Assyrian capital, has fallen to the Babylonians and ⟦l:media_776|Medes⟧, an event the prophet ⟦p:nahum_2145|Nahum⟧ celebrated. ⟦p:pharaoh-nechoh_2337|Pharaoh Neco⟧ of ⟦l:egypt_362|Egypt⟧ marches north to support what is left of ⟦l:assyria_111|Assyria⟧ against ⟦l:babylon_151|Babylon⟧, and ⟦p:josiah_1730|Josiah⟧ goes out to meet him at ⟦l:megiddo_777|Megiddo⟧. Afterwards, Egypt controls ⟦l:judah-southern_1281|Judah⟧, and ⟦p:pharaoh-nechoh_2337|Neco⟧ chooses who will sit on ⟦p:david_994|David⟧'s throne.
24:
⟦p:josiah_1730|Josiah⟧ is dead, and Judah is now a vassal of ⟦l:egypt_362|Egypt⟧. ⟦p:pharaoh-nechoh_2337|Pharaoh Neco⟧ has deposed Josiah's son ⟦p:ahaziah_121|Jehoahaz⟧ after three months and placed another son, ⟦p:jehoiakim_1085|Eliakim⟧, on the throne under the new name ⟦p:jehoiakim_1085|Jehoiakim⟧. But the balance of power is about to shift again. At Carchemish on the ⟦l:euphrates_421|Euphrates⟧, around six hundred and five years before Christ, the Babylonian crown prince ⟦p:nebuchadnezzar_2167|Nebuchadnezzar⟧ defeats the Egyptian army, and soon afterwards he becomes king of ⟦l:babylon_151|Babylon⟧. Egypt, the writer notes, never marched out of its own land again.

⟦p:jehoiakim_1085|Jehoiakim⟧ submits to ⟦l:babylon_151|Babylon⟧ for three years and then rebels. The book of ⟦p:jeremiah_848|Jeremiah⟧ gives a vivid picture of this king, who cut up the prophet's scroll and burned it piece by piece in his winter fire. The book of ⟦p:daniel_975|Daniel⟧ places the first deportation of young nobles to Babylon in his reign. Jehoiakim dies before ⟦p:nebuchadnezzar_2167|Nebuchadnezzar⟧'s army reaches ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧, and the blow falls instead on his eighteen-year-old son ⟦p:jehoiachin_791|Jehoiachin⟧.

⟦p:jehoiachin_791|Jehoiachin⟧ reigns only three months before ⟦p:nebuchadnezzar_2167|Nebuchadnezzar⟧'s army surrounds ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧. This first fall of the city, about five hundred and ninety-seven years before Christ, strips it of its king, its leaders, its soldiers and its craftsmen. Among those carried to ⟦l:babylon_151|Babylon⟧ was a priest named ⟦p:ezekiel_1237|Ezekiel⟧, who would receive his visions among the exiles. Nebuchadnezzar places Jehoiachin's uncle on the throne, another son of ⟦p:josiah_1730|Josiah⟧, renaming him ⟦p:zedekiah_1950|Zedekiah⟧. He will be the last king of Judah.
25:
⟦p:zedekiah_1950|Zedekiah⟧ has rebelled against ⟦l:babylon_151|Babylon⟧, despite the warnings of ⟦p:jeremiah_853|Jeremiah⟧, whose book tells these final years from inside the city, with the prophet imprisoned and consulted in secret by the frightened king.

The chapter is dated with care, almost day by day. In the ninth year of ⟦p:zedekiah_1950|Zedekiah⟧'s reign, ⟦p:nebuchadnezzar_2167|Nebuchadnezzar⟧'s army arrives and builds siege works around ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧. The siege lasts about a year and a half, until famine has done its work. What happens to Zedekiah takes place at ⟦l:riblah_1001|Riblah⟧, in ⟦l:syria_1122|Syria⟧, where Nebuchadnezzar has his headquarters, and the destruction of the city is carried out a month later by his captain of the guard, ⟦p:nebuzar-adan_2169|Nebuzaradan⟧. Among the things broken up and carried away are the bronze pillars, the stands and the great Sea that ⟦p:solomon_2762|Solomon⟧'s craftsman made.

The account does not end with the burning of the city. ⟦p:nebuchadnezzar_2167|Nebuchadnezzar⟧ appoints a governor over those left in the land, ⟦p:gedaliah_1287|Gedaliah⟧, the grandson of ⟦p:shaphan_2550|Shaphan⟧, the secretary who read the book of the law to ⟦p:josiah_1730|Josiah⟧. Then the final paragraph moves forward many years, to ⟦l:babylon_151|Babylon⟧, where ⟦p:jehoiachin_791|Jehoiachin⟧, the king taken captive as a young man, is still alive in prison. Clay tablets found in Babylon record the rations issued to him there. The last word of the book belongs to him, a son of ⟦p:david_994|David⟧.
